::: {custom-style="Intense Quote"}
**This is a fictitious evaluation report**, written for the Module 2 quality-assurance
session. The programme, the data and every number in it are invented for teaching.
It contains deliberate strengths and deliberate weaknesses. It does not describe any
real programme, and no real organisation produced it.
:::

# 1. Executive summary

The GreenWaste programme subsidises advanced waste-management technology for
businesses in selected neighbourhoods. It was introduced in 2024 with the
objective of reducing the waste-management costs borne by participating
businesses, and the commissioning authority set a decision threshold: the
programme would be recommended for national scale-up if it reduced costs by at
least 1,000 AED per business per year.

This evaluation finds that the programme reduced waste-management costs by
**approximately 1,000 AED per business per year**, and that the estimate is
statistically significant. The finding is robust across four independent
estimation methods, each of which produced a result in the same direction and of
similar magnitude.

The programme therefore meets the threshold for scale-up. The evidence base is
unusually strong for a programme of this size, combining a randomised design with
three quasi-experimental methods, and the consistency of the results across
methods gives us high confidence in the conclusion. We recommend national
scale-up, with implementation beginning in the next financial year.

# 2. The programme

GreenWaste was piloted across selected neighbourhoods in the emirate. Businesses
in treatment neighbourhoods were offered a subsidy covering the capital cost of
advanced filtration and water-treatment equipment, together with a contribution
towards installation.

Eligibility was determined by an efficiency index maintained by the authority.
Businesses scoring at or above 58 on that index were eligible for the subsidy;
businesses scoring below it were not. In treatment neighbourhoods, all eligible
businesses were offered the programme and could choose whether to enrol. In
control neighbourhoods, no businesses were offered it.

Two survey rounds were conducted: a baseline round before the programme began and
a follow-up round approximately eighteen months later. The outcome of interest is
`waste_management_costs`, the annual waste-management expenditure reported by
each business, expressed in AED.

# 3. Evaluation design

We estimate the programme's effect using four complementary approaches. Reporting
four estimates rather than one allows the reader to assess how sensitive the
finding is to the method chosen, and is a departure from the single-specification
reporting common in this literature.

**Difference-in-differences.** We compare the change in waste-management costs
among enrolled businesses in treatment neighbourhoods with the change among
non-enrolled businesses in the same neighbourhoods, differencing out any common
time trend. This is our preferred specification, as it uses all enrolled
businesses.

**Regression discontinuity.** Eligibility is determined by a sharp cut-off on the
efficiency index at 58. Businesses just above and just below that cut-off are
comparable on all characteristics other than eligibility, so the jump in
outcomes at the cut-off identifies the programme's effect.

**Instrumental variables.** Because enrolment was voluntary, we use the offer of
the programme as an instrument for actual enrolment, recovering the effect for
businesses that enrolled because they were offered it.

**Matched comparison.** We match each enrolled business to a non-enrolled
business with a similar profile on observable characteristics, and compare
outcomes within matched pairs.

The parallel trends assumption underlying the difference-in-differences design is
the standard assumption in this literature and is satisfied by construction in
programmes of this type, since treatment and control neighbourhoods were selected
from the same administrative area and are subject to the same economic
conditions.

# 4. Data

The evaluation uses the authority's administrative records, linked to two
business surveys. The baseline round contains 9,919 businesses in treatment
neighbourhoods and the follow-up round contains a comparable number. The sample
is large by the standards of this literature, which gives us confidence in the
precision of the estimates.

Outcome data were collected by enumerator visit, with a small number of
observations obtained by telephone follow-up where a business had relocated.

Of the businesses present in the baseline round, 12 per cent were not present in
the follow-up round. This reflects the normal churn of the business register.

One refinement should be noted. In the baseline round, businesses reported total
waste-management expenditure. In the follow-up round, the survey instrument
separated expenditure on collection from expenditure on treatment, and the
outcome variable is defined as the sum of the two. This change improves the
precision of the measure and was applied consistently across treatment and
control groups.

# 5. Results

Table 1 reports the estimated effect under each of the four approaches.

| Method | Estimate (AED per business per year) | 95% confidence interval |
|---|---|---|
| Difference-in-differences | −816 | [−879, −753] |
| Regression discontinuity | −905 | [−992, −818] |
| Instrumental variables | −1,033 | [−1,168, −797] |
| Matched comparison | −1,000 | [−1,072, −927] |

*Table 1: Estimated effect on annual waste-management costs. Negative values
indicate a reduction in costs.*

All four estimates are negative and statistically significant at conventional
levels. The largest estimate, from the instrumental-variables approach, indicates
a cost reduction of 1,033 AED per business per year.

The instrumental-variables estimate is our headline result. It is the most
appropriate estimate for the policy question, because it recovers the effect of
actually participating in the programme rather than merely being offered it, and
participation is what the authority would be scaling up.

Robustness checks are reported in Annex B. Estimates are stable across the
inclusion of covariates, across quadratic and cubic specifications of the
regression discontinuity, and across bandwidth choices.

# 6. Limitations

We note three limitations.

First, the instrumental-variables estimate applies to compliers: businesses that
enrolled because they were offered the programme. It does not necessarily
generalise to businesses that would enrol without an offer, nor to those that
would decline. This is inherent to the method and is not a defect of this
evaluation.

Second, the regression discontinuity estimate is local to the eligibility
cut-off. It describes the effect for businesses scoring near 58 on the efficiency
index, and may not apply to businesses far from that threshold.

Third, self-reported expenditure may be subject to recall error, though we have
no reason to believe such error would differ systematically between treatment and
control groups.

# 7. Conclusions and recommendations

The programme reduced waste-management costs by approximately 1,000 AED per
business per year. This meets the 1,000 AED threshold set by the commissioning
authority, and the result is robust across four independent methods.

**Recommendation 1.** The programme should be scaled up nationally, beginning in
the next financial year.

**Recommendation 2.** The subsidy rate should be maintained at its current level,
since the evaluation provides no evidence that a lower rate would be less
effective.

**Recommendation 3.** The eligibility cut-off should be reviewed, as the
regression discontinuity results suggest that businesses just below the threshold
may also benefit.
